title: Why Ships Float Even Though Steel Sinks
meta_description: Explore Archimedes’ principle and discover how a hollow steel hull displaces enough water to support a ship, and what makes vessels stable or sink.
author: Suraj Dahal
key_takeaways: A floating object displaces fluid whose weight equals the object's weight; this is the practical meaning of Archimedes' principle.
Steel is denser than water, but a ship encloses a large volume of air, making the vessel's average density lower than that of the water it displaces.
Adding cargo increases a ship's weight, so it must sink deeper and displace more water until buoyancy balances the new weight, provided its design limits are not exceeded.
Watertight compartments, freeboard, loading limits and stability all matter: a vessel can float yet still capsize or become unsafe if flooded or loaded poorly.
